name: Dip
standfirst: A dip is a texture before it is a recipe: something soft enough to give way under bread and salty enough that you keep going back. Four decisions make every one of them — what gets pulped, what fat carries it, what sour cuts the fat, and how far you take the pounding. Change nothing about burnt aubergine except the fat you beat into it and you have left Beirut for Tehran.
root: Something soft or softened · broken down with salt and garlic in a mortar or a machine · slackened with a fat and cut with something sour · eaten cold with bread

dishes.name: Tahini sauce

base: a nut or seed
sesame already ground to a paste
nothing pulped into it at all
fat: the seed's own oil and no other
acid: poured in until the paste seizes solid
cold water after it to bring it back
body: whisked in a bowl by hand
thin enough to pour off a spoon

dishes.note: The plainest thing here and the one two others are built on: sesame paste, garlic crushed with salt, lemon, water. It is a sauce for fish and falafel on its own, and it is the medium that hummus and mutabbal are suspended in.

dishes.name: Hummus

region: Beirut and Damascus and Jerusalem all claim it
base: a cooked pulse
chickpeas simmered soft with bicarbonate
the skins slipped off by hand
fat: tahini beaten in until the whole thing pales
olive oil poured over at the table
acid: beaten in with the tahini rather than after
body: run through a food mill or pounded
whipped with iced water until it lifts

dishes.note: Hummus bi tahina is the full name and it is an instruction: this is tahini sauce with chickpeas beaten into it. That is why it sits underneath rather than beside. The skins are the only thing standing between a good one and a great one.

dishes.name: Mutabbal

base: a cooked vegetable
aubergine burnt whole over a flame
the flesh hung to drain its bitter water
fat: yogurt as well in some houses
acid: enough to keep the tahini pale
body: mashed with a fork rather than blended
kept loose enough to swirl in the dish

dishes.note: The same sauce again with smoke instead of starch under it. Mutabbal means spiced or seasoned; what defines it against its neighbour is that the tahini goes in, and what defines it against hummus is that the flame does the cooking.

dishes.name: Baba ganoush

base: a cooked vegetable
aubergine burnt whole over a flame
the flesh chopped rather than pulped
fat: poured over rather than beaten in
body: chopped on a board with a knife
tomato and green pepper cut through it

dishes.note: In the West this name has been swallowed by mutabbal and now means the tahini one. At home it is the other fork off the same burnt aubergine: no sesame, a fruit acid instead of lemon alone, and knifework instead of a mortar — a salad rather than a paste.

dishes.name: Kashk-e bademjan

base: a cooked vegetable
aubergine fried in oil until gold
onion fried down to brown with it
fat: the aubergine drinks it in the pan
dried mint bloomed in more oil and poured over
acid: kashk stirred through and drizzled on top
sour by fermentation rather than by fruit
body: pounded in a mortar but stopped short of a paste

dishes.note: Aubergine again with every other decision moved. The sour is kashk — drained yogurt fermented and dried to rocks then let down with water — so the acid and a second fat arrive in the same spoonful. Frying rather than burning means it tastes of oil and onion instead of smoke.

dishes.name: Ajvar

base: a cooked vegetable
red peppers roasted until the skins lift
aubergine for about a third of the weight
fat: sunflower oil cooked into it over hours
a last film on top to seal the jar
acid: a splash at the very end
it is the preservative as much as the seasoning
body: cooked down until a spoon will stand in it

dishes.note: The only one here that is cooked after it is pulped and the only one made by the bucket in September. Everything else is a dish; ajvar is a winter store that happens to be eaten with bread.

dishes.name: Nam phrik num

base: a cooked vegetable
long green chillies charred in the embers
shallots and garlic charred in their skins
fat: nothing poured in and nothing beaten in
acid: fish sauce carries the salt instead
body: loose enough to pick up with sticky rice

dishes.note: The proof that the fat is optional and the pounding is not. Charring the chillies and aromatics whole before they meet the pestle is the same move as burning an aubergine over a flame — sweetness and smoke bought before anything is crushed.

dishes.name: Muhammara

base: a nut or seed
walnuts pounded coarse
roasted red pepper pounded in with them
fat: olive oil worked in as well
body: breadcrumbs stirred in to give it body

dishes.note: Muhammara means reddened. The walnut is the base rather than a garnish, which is why it is grainy in the mouth where its neighbours are creamy — and why the acid has to be pomegranate: lemon alone cannot get through that much oil.

dishes.name: Coconut chutney

base: a nut or seed
fresh coconut grated off the shell
roasted gram dal ground in with it
fat: coconut oil heated for the tempering
mustard seed and curry leaf fried and poured on top
acid: yogurt instead of it in some houses
body: ground on a wet stone with water

dishes.note: The only one whose last move happens in a hot pan after the grinding is done: seeds and leaves fried in oil and tipped over the top so they crackle. Made fresh each morning because coconut turns by evening.

dishes.name: Ful medames

base: a cooked pulse
fava beans simmered overnight in a narrow pot
cumin ground over them
fat: poured over at the table by the eater
tahini stirred in in some houses
acid: squeezed on at the last moment
body: crushed against the side of the pot with a spoon

dishes.note: Breakfast rather than a mezze, and the one dip nobody finishes making in the kitchen — the oil and lemon go on in front of you, and how far it gets mashed is decided by whoever is holding the bread.

dishes.name: Tzatziki

base: milk drained or soured
yogurt strained through cloth
cucumber grated and wrung out dry
acid: a spoonful of vinegar in some houses

dishes.note: The only base here that arrived already sour, so no acid needs pouring in. Wringing the cucumber is the whole technique: skip it and the salt pulls the water out on the table instead and you get soup.

dishes.name: Tirokafteri

base: milk drained or soured
feta broken up in the bowl
a roasted chilli beaten in with it
fat: olive oil beaten in until it pales
acid: the brine it was kept in
body: beaten hard until it holds air

dishes.note: Whipped feta, and the beating is the point — htipiti, its other name, simply means beaten. No water and no lemon could make feta this pale; it is air, the same trick as whipping butter.

dishes.name: Salsa huancaína

region: named for Huancayo in the Andes
base: milk drained or soured
queso fresco crumbled in
ají amarillo fried soft and blended with it
fat: a little oil to hold the blend together
acid: the salt of the cheese does that work instead
body: blended with soda crackers where it needs body
thin enough to pour over cold potatoes

dishes.note: Fresh cheese standing in for yogurt on a continent with no yogurt tradition. It is poured over boiled potatoes as often as it is scooped — the same paste asked to be a sauce, which is what happens when you keep thinning a dip.

dishes.name: Skordalia

base: a starch
potato boiled and passed through a ricer
stale bread soaked and squeezed in other houses
fat: worked in a thread at a time like mayonnaise
walnuts or almonds pounded in on some islands
acid: lemon juice instead of it in some houses
body: the garlic pounded to a paste with salt before anything else
stiff enough to stand a spoon in

dishes.note: Named for the garlic and not for the potato, which tells you which one is the dish. The starch is only there to hold oil — take it away and drip the oil into the garlic alone and you have Lebanese toum instead.

dishes.name: Taramasalata

region: and the Greek kitchens of Istanbul
base: cured fish roe
salted carp or cod roe
soaked bread or riced potato beaten in with it
fat: beaten in drop by drop like mayonnaise
a neutral oil in part so it does not fight the roe
acid: added by turns with the oil
body: beaten until it turns pale and doubles
a mousse rather than a paste

dishes.note: The only savoury base here that was preserved before it was pulped, and the only one that is a true emulsion — the roe holds the oil the way an egg yolk does. The bread is a brake as much as a bulker: it stops the thing splitting.

dishes.name: Guacamole

base: a raw fruit
avocado scooped from the skin
chilli and onion ground to a paste first
acid: it also holds off the browning

dishes.note: The only base that is neither cooked nor cured nor fermented, and the only one that brings its own fat in the flesh. Grinding the chilli and onion before the avocado goes in is the order that matters — afterwards you would only be bruising it.

notes.title: On the four decisions
notes.body: What is pulped sets the flavour, but it is the other three that place the dish on a map. The fat is the carrier — sesame paste, olive oil, a seed oil, the fat already inside a walnut or an avocado, or none at all. The sour is what stops the fat being dull, and it is the most local decision of the four: lemon in the Levant, lime in Mexico and northern Thailand, vinegar in the Balkans, pomegranate in Aleppo, fermented whey in Iran, and in tzatziki nothing added because the base soured itself. Burnt aubergine with tahini and lemon is mutabbal; the same aubergine fried and finished with kashk is Iranian; chopped instead of pounded with pomegranate molasses is baba ganoush. One vegetable and three countries.

notes.title: On what tahini does
notes.body: Sesame paste is an emulsion looking for an excuse to break. Pour lemon juice into it and it seizes — stiffens into something like plaster — because the acid drops the pH and the protein grabs the water. Beat cold water in after that and it comes back, but paler and thicker than it started. That seizing and recovery is the texture of hummus and of mutabbal; it is why both are white rather than beige, and why neither can be made properly by simply stirring everything together at once.

notes.title: On the mortar and the machine
notes.body: Smooth or chunky is mostly a decision about the tool, and the tool is usually older than the recipe. A basalt molcajete crushes against a rough face and leaves lumps, which is why guacamole has them. A stone mortar and a pestle can be stopped anywhere between coarse and paste, which is how muhammara and nam phrik num stay grainy. A food mill takes the skins out and gives no air, which is what hummus wants. A blender whips air in, which is what tirokafteri and taramasalata want and what ruins hummus. The blender is the only one that changes colour as well as texture.

notes.title: On depth
notes.body: Only hummus and mutabbal sit underneath another dish, because both genuinely are tahini sauce plus a pulped thing — you make the sauce first and beat the chickpeas or the aubergine into it, and hummus bi tahina says so in its name. Everything else stands at the same level. Baba ganoush is not mutabbal with the tahini taken out: it is chopped rather than pounded and soured with pomegranate, a different dish from the same vegetable. Salsa huancaína is not a Peruvian tirokafteri, and coconut chutney is not an Indian muhammara. They are separate answers to the same question, and hanging one under the other would make the tree tidier and the claim false.

notes.title: On what is not here
notes.body: Fresh things cut with a knife are salsas, not dips: pico de gallo, Turkish ezme, Ethiopian awaze fresca. The line is that a salsa is chopped and stays wet and separate, while a dip is broken down until it holds together and holds a piece of bread up. Toum is left out for the opposite reason — it is skordalia with the starch removed, garlic and oil and nothing pulped, which puts it among the emulsified sauces with aioli. And ful medames sits at the edge of the family on purpose: it is the one that is still being made while you eat it.
